chief_complaint: severe shortness of breath when lying flat, waking up choking, and morning headaches for 6 months
hpi_details: 6-month history of intense, debilitating shortness of breath that occurs almost immediately upon lying flat on his back in bed (severe orthopnoea). Within 60 seconds of assuming a supine position, he feels as though his chest is being crushed and he cannot draw air into his lungs, forcing him to sleep sitting bolt upright in a recliner chair every night. Also experiences paradoxical worsening of dyspnoea when swimming in a pool or bending over to tie his shoes. Wakes up every morning with a dull frontal headache and severe unexhausted fatigue due to shallow nighttime breathing. Can walk on flat ground at a slow pace without severe distress. Has a history of type 2 diabetes and underwent a difficult, prolonged upper abdominal open cholecystectomy surgery 1 year ago where the surgeon noted difficulty stopping bleeding around the diaphragm.
ideas: thinks his heart is failing or fluid is filling his lungs every time he lies down
concerns: terrified he will fall asleep lying flat and suffocate to death in his bed
expectations: wants heart failure water pills and a breathing machine that lets him sleep lying down
pmh: open cholecystectomy with difficult surgical course 1 year ago, type 2 diabetes mellitus
social_hx: never smoked, zero alcohol, retired accountant, lives with wife

clinical_knowledge.topic: Bilateral diaphragmatic paralysis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Bilateral diaphragmatic weakness can cause marked orthopnoea, sleep-related hypoventilation, morning headaches, and positional oxygen desaturation despite relatively preserved upright function.
A history of upper abdominal, thoracic, or neck surgery can support phrenic nerve injury, but other neuromuscular, inflammatory, and idiopathic causes must be considered.

Compare upright and supine vital capacity; a substantial fall when supine supports diaphragmatic weakness. Dynamic ultrasound, fluoroscopy, and respiratory specialist assessment can help confirm the diagnosis.
Management prioritizes assessment for hypercapnic respiratory failure and nocturnal hypoventilation, treatment of any reversible cause, and specialist-directed ventilatory support when indicated.
diagnostic_clues: Immediate, severe breathlessness on lying supine, with relief when upright
Morning headaches and unrefreshing sleep suggesting nocturnal hypoventilation
Worsening dyspnoea when bending forward or swimming
Previous difficult upper abdominal surgery, a potential phrenic nerve injury mechanism
Positional desaturation, paradoxical abdominal movement when supine, elevated hemidiaphragms, and a substantial supine fall in forced vital capacity
common_misconceptions: Assuming orthopnoea always represents heart failure without considering diaphragmatic or neuromuscular causes.
Using upright spirometry alone to exclude diaphragmatic weakness.
Attributing morning headaches and fatigue to anxiety without assessing for nocturnal hypoventilation.
dangerous_errors: Missing acute or worsening hypercapnic respiratory failure, hypoxaemia, or inability to maintain ventilation when supine.
Prescribing sedatives or other respiratory depressants without evaluating ventilatory reserve.
Delaying urgent respiratory assessment in a patient with escalating breathlessness, somnolence, or bulbar symptoms.
management_principles: Assess gas exchange and sleep-related hypoventilation, and obtain respiratory specialist input for significant positional or nocturnal symptoms.
Treat a reversible cause when identified; nocturnal non-invasive ventilation may be appropriate after specialist assessment for symptomatic hypoventilation.
Avoid respiratory depressants when possible and give clear escalation advice for worsening breathlessness or drowsiness.
boundaries_and_exceptions: The diagnosis requires clinical correlation; imaging and positional pulmonary-function findings are supportive rather than independently definitive.
The choice of ventilatory support, monitoring setting, and any surgical intervention requires respiratory and specialist multidisciplinary assessment.

source_refs.title: Bilateral diaphragmatic paralysis: respiratory specialist evaluation

reference_soap.subjective: 57M post-upper abdominal surgery presents with 6-month severe immediate orthopnoea, water immersion dyspnoea, morning headaches, and sleep disruption. No orthopnoea delay or cardiac murmurs.
reference_soap.objective: Perform targeted physical and respiratory physiology assessment. Vitals: O2 sat 96% while sitting upright on room air, dropping precipitously to 87% within 2 minutes of lying flat supine. Abdominal/Chest inspection: observe respiration -> while sitting, breathing appears normal; while lying supine, exhibits dramatic Paradoxical Abdominal Respiration (during inspiration, the anterior abdominal wall indraws/sinks inward while the chest expands, indicating complete failure and upward suction of both hemidiaphragms). Pulmonary Function Tests (Spirometry -> CRITICAL POSITION-DEPENDENT TESTING): measure FVC sitting upright (e.g., 2.8 Litres) and immediately repeat FVC lying supine -> demonstrates a severe, pathognomonic drop in Forced Vital Capacity of >30% (often 40-50% drop down to 1.5 Litres when supine; normal individuals show <10% drop). Erect Posteroanterior and Lateral Chest X-ray: reveals marked, symmetrical elevation of both right and left hemidiaphragms accompanied by basal subsegmental atelectasis. Fluoroscopic Sniff Test (or dynamic ultrasound): confirms complete absence of downward diaphragmatic excursion or paradoxical upward movement during vigorous sniffing.
reference_soap.assessment: Bilateral Diaphragmatic Paralysis secondary to bilateral phrenic nerve injury during complicated open upper abdominal surgery (or neuralgic amyotrophy / idiopathic), leading to severe postural orthopnoea and nocturnal alveolar hypoventilation. DDx: Congestive Heart Failure (causes delayed orthopnoea after 15-30 minutes due to venous redistribution, accompanied by elevated JVP/S3 gallop and normal supine FVC), severe COPD, motor neuron disease / ALS (check for limb wasting/fasciculations), morbid obesity hypoventilation syndrome.
reference_soap.plan: Explain the suspected diaphragmatic mechanism while evaluating cardiac and other causes of orthopnoea. Assess urgently for hypercapnia and hypoxaemia; emergency evaluation is needed for respiratory distress, worsening drowsiness or confusion, or inability to maintain ventilation when supine. Avoid sedatives and other respiratory depressants where possible. A respiratory specialist may arrange sleep assessment and initiate nocturnal non-invasive ventilation if indicated; consider multidisciplinary thoracic-surgery review only for persistent, carefully selected cases.

learning_objectives: Differentiate Bilateral Diaphragmatic Paralysis (immediate supine dyspnoea with paradoxical inward abdominal inspiration) from cardiac orthopnoea
Interpret position-dependent spirometry, where a marked fall in Forced Vital Capacity from sitting to supine supports diaphragmatic weakness
Interpret fluoroscopic sniff testing and chest X-ray demonstrating bilateral hemidiaphragm elevation and paradoxical excursion
Recognize when urgent respiratory assessment and specialist-directed nocturnal ventilatory support may be needed

teaching.one_liner: Immediate severe orthopnoea with sleep-related hypoventilation and a history suggesting bilateral phrenic nerve injury.
differentials: Motor neuron disease or another neuromuscular disorder
COPD or another obstructive lung disease
red_flags: Worsening drowsiness, confusion, or severe morning headache suggesting hypercapnia
Hypoxaemia, respiratory distress, or inability to lie supine
New dysphagia, weak cough, or other progressive neuromuscular symptoms

must_ask.say: How quickly does your breathlessness begin after you lie flat, and does sitting upright relieve it?
Do you wake with headaches, poor sleep, unusual sleepiness, or episodes of choking at night?
Did your breathing begin after any neck, chest, or upper abdominal surgery, injury, or infection?
Have you noticed limb weakness, muscle twitching, trouble swallowing, or a weak cough?
Do you have leg swelling, chest pain, fever, wheeze, or a known heart or lung disease?
